owner: xlog baseline — mainstream shorts conventions + pilot creator reference (LoL commentary style)

criteria.name: hook_strength
criteria.description: The opening must stop the scroll immediately: cold-open on the highest-action / highest-emotion moment with no title card or pre-roll, and land the first caption line within the first ~0.5s as an unresolved claim or question that only completes in the next line. For live-action narrative footage, a peak-emotion face plus visible physical evidence (bruise, grip, tears) beats a detail/object insert as the 0s frame. Judged over the first 3 seconds.

criteria.name: mainstream_convention
criteria.description: Follows proven, broadly appealing Shorts/Reels conventions for caption placement, structure, and readability. Safe beats experimental — except that the creator's reference establishes narration-subtitle-driven, letterboxed gameplay commentary as an accepted house form; do not penalize long uncut takes or 16:9-in-9:16 letterboxing on their own. Slightly long shots (3–4.5s) are acceptable when each one carries new visible information.

criteria.name: instruction_fit
criteria.description: Faithfully realizes the user's free-form request (caption tone, effects, mood). When the brief asks for subtitles, near-every-beat captioning is expected and a run of silent shots is a real miss. Ignore this criterion (redistribute judgment) when no request was given.

criteria.name: pacing
criteria.description: No dead air and energy rising toward the payoff. Perceived pace may come from subtitle turnover (one short line every 1–2s) over long uncut takes rather than from frequent hard cuts; deliberate rhythm breaks (e.g., a mid-roll still interlude, one caption-free breath before the payoff) are welcome when they set up a payoff. Tighter cutting alone does not outrank a clearer, better-grounded arc.

criteria.name: narrative_clarity
criteria.description: One clear thread from hook to payoff; no confusing jumps. The strongest shape is question → clue → reveal: the hook poses a question, each following shot releases one new visible clue, and the payoff answers it with a concrete detail rather than restating the premise. Every caption must be anchored to something actually visible in the frame — inferred or atmospheric assertions the footage does not show are a clarity defect, not a stylistic choice. Silent visual interludes are fine when they restate the narration's point rather than introduce a new one.

criteria.name: moment_selection
criteria.description: The genuinely best raw moments were used, not filler. Prefer shots that contain concrete, readable evidence (faces at peak emotion, hands, marks, revealed names/objects) over connective coverage such as low-angle feet, wide walking, or empty-space shots.

preferences: Open cold on the highest-action / highest-emotion moment of the clip and place the first subtitle line within the first 0.5 seconds, phrased as an incomplete claim or question that only resolves later.

For live-action narrative footage, structure the edit as question → clue → reveal: hook on a peak-emotion face close-up that poses the question, release one new visible clue per shot, and pay it off with a concrete detail shot that answers it.

Caption only what is literally visible in the frame (a bruise, a hand gripping an arm, a name tattooed on skin); avoid interpretive or atmospheric lines that assert things the footage does not show — let the viewer supply the emotion.
When the brief asks for subtitles, keep a caption on nearly every beat; reserve silent shots for the one breath before the payoff and the final loop cut.
Keep gameplay in long uncut takes and generate pace with subtitle turnover instead of cuts — swap one short caption line every 1–2 seconds, one spoken clause per line.
Burn captions as bold white text on a soft dark translucent plate, centered in the lower third and above the game HUD, never covering the minimap or item bar.
Letterbox the 16:9 gameplay in a 9:16 frame and keep the crop centered on the champion so the black bars double as caption space.
Insert one silent full-bleed meme/still interlude around the 55–70% mark that visually restates the narration's joke, holding each still 2–3 seconds.
Join interlude stills with 0.5–1s dip-to-black fades rather than hard cuts, and drop all captions during the interlude so the image carries the gag.
Drop captions during the peak action beat so the payoff can breathe.
End on a short self-deprecating reaction caption over live action and fade to black mid-play instead of using an outro card.
Avoid emojis and on-screen title cards.
notes: v3 — first non-gameplay (live-action narrative) comparison. User picked A, agreeing with the primary judge but for a different stated reason: '조금 더 객관적인 사실을 보여줌' — A's captions and reveals point at things actually visible in frame (bruise, grip, the MATHEW tattoo), while B leans on interpretive/atmospheric lines ('조명은 점점 좁아지고', '도망칠 곳은 없다'). Note this directly contradicts the second opinion, which called A's tattoo reveal speculative; the creator treats a shown detail as fact, so evidence-in-frame outranks a critic's doubt about story inference. Changes: narrative_clarity 10→12 and mainstream_convention 20→18 (small nudge, one data point) to reflect that grounded, evidence-anchored arcs matter more than the safest stylistic template; narrative_clarity now requires every caption to be anchored to visible content and names question→clue→reveal as the preferred shape; moment_selection now explicitly downranks connective coverage (low-angle feet, wide walking); hook_strength adds that a peak-emotion face plus visible physical evidence beats a detail insert at 0s for live-action; instruction_fit and pacing note that near-every-beat captioning is expected when subtitles are briefed and that tighter cutting alone does not outrank a clearer arc. Three new preferences distilled (evidence-only captions, question→clue→reveal structure for live-action, caption density under a subtitle brief); gameplay-specific house-style preferences retained unchanged since they were not exercised here.
